title: What makes PFAS so persistent? The C–F bond explained
description: Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances persist in the environment because of one extraordinary chemical property: the carbon–fluorine bond. This post unpacks why it is so difficult to break, and how microbial enzymes might finally offer a solution.
body:
The carbon–fluorine bond is the strongest bond in organic chemistry. At ~130 kcal/mol and just 1.35 Å in length, it resists almost every chemical and biological degradation pathway that nature has evolved over billions of years.

## Why fluorine is exceptional

PFAS compounds exploit this property: fluorine atoms shield the carbon backbone with a belt of electronegativity, repelling nucleophilic attack and blocking oxidative enzymes. The result is a class of chemicals that can persist in soil and water for over a millennium.

Three properties make the C–F bond so resistant:

- **Bond strength**: ~130 kcal/mol, compared to ~99 kcal/mol for C–H
- **Bond length**: only 1.35 Å, the shortest carbon bond in organic chemistry
- **Electronegativity**: fluorine (3.98) is the most electronegative element, creating a permanent dipole that repels attacking nucleophiles

## How our lab approaches the problem

Our lab focuses on finding the rare microbial enzymes, dehalogenases, that have evolved the active-site geometry to destabilise and ultimately cleave this bond.

The challenge is not just finding them; it is understanding *why* they work so that we can engineer them to be faster, broader in substrate scope, and robust enough for real-world remediation.

## The discovery pipeline

We use a four-stage approach:

- **Metagenomic sequencing**: capturing environmental DNA from contaminated sites
- **Bioinformatic mining**: scanning millions of sequences for dehalogenase signatures
- **Structural prediction**: using AlphaFold and Boltz-2 to model active sites
- **Lab validation**: confirming computational leads with biochemical assays

The goal is a scalable, enzymatic solution to PFAS contamination: one that works under environmentally relevant conditions without generating toxic by-products.
